rationale: A wins because it is more disciplined about the holes in the update, especially in "Warby Parker got profitable. Now it is spending on 40 stores and optometrists." B has sharper packaging, but "The poster child of online-only retail now runs more than 300 stores" leans on outside DTC mythology the update did not supply. A has one padded data angle, but B's biggest swing is also its biggest grounding problem.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker says store shoppers spend more than online buyers. It will not say how much." is kept as a standalone data angle even though, without the number, it is closer to a proof request than a story.
"The company that made direct-to-consumer eyewear a category" is useful context, but it is not in the supplied update and should be verified or softened.
"puts pressure on whoever currently sells eyewear in pharmacies and on incumbent optical chains" speculates about competitive impact the update does not establish.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker was the canonical example of that thesis" is an outside historical claim, not a supplied fact. If it is wrong or stale, the whole lead angle wobbles.
"the death of a retail thesis" is too big for the evidence. Forty stores and 300-plus total stores do not kill a thesis by themselves.
"pharmacy chains' fight to reinvent the front of store" invents a broader retail peg the update did not provide.
"Several states restrict corporate employment of optometrists" may be a smart diligence question, but it injects a regulatory fact after refusing fabricated regulatory angles elsewhere.
